etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English trial, triall, from Anglo-Norman trial, triel, from trier (“to pick out, cull”) + -al. More at English try.

definitions.definition: The testing of a product or procedure.
(medicine, sciences, research) A research study to test the effectiveness and safety of a drug, medical procedure, etc.
An event in which athletes’ or animals’ abilities are tested as they compete for a place on a team, or to move on to the next level of a championship, for example.
(ceramics) A piece of ware used to test the heat of a kiln.
(UK) An internal examination set by Eton College.
(archaic) An occasion on which armies or individuals meet in combat.

quote.citation: c. 1597, William Shakespeare, Henry IV, Part 1‎[4], Act V, Scene 1:
quote.text: In both your armies there is many a soul / Shall pay full dearly for this encounter, / If once they join in trial.

definitions.definition: An occasion on which a person or thing is tested to find out how well they perform or how suitable they are.

quote.citation: c. 1611, William Shakespeare, The Tempest‎[1], Act IV, Scene 1:
quote.text: all thy vexations / Were but my trials of thy love and thou / Hast strangely stood the test here

quote.citation: 1847, Anne Brontë, chapter 3, in Agnes Grey‎[2], London: Thomas Cautley Newby, page 51:
quote.text: had my powers been less limited, I might have enforced obedience; but as it was, it was but a trial of strength between her and me, in which she generally came off victorious

quote.citation: 2010, Nadifa Mohamed, Black Mamba Boy‎[3], Harper Collins, page 65:
quote.text: Jama saw the sweaty, smelly work as a kind of test that, if passed, would entitle him to see his father, a trial of his worth as a son and as a man.

definitions.definition: A meeting or series of meetings in a court of law at which evidence is presented to a judge (and sometimes a jury) to allow them to decide on a legal matter (especially whether an accused person is guilty of a crime).

quote.citation: c. 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Winters Tale”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iii]:
quote.text: as she hath / Been publicly accused, so shall she have / A just and open trial

quote.citation: 1847, Henry Wadsworth Longfellow, Evangeline‎[5], Boston: Ticknor, Part 3, p. 42:
quote.text: She, after form of trial condemned to die on the scaffold, / Patiently met her doom at the foot of the statue of Justice.

quote.citation: 1960, Harper Lee, chapter 20, in To Kill a Mockingbird‎[6], Philadelphia: Lippincott, page 215:
quote.text: […]  this case should never have come to trial.

quote.citation: 2020, Charles Yu, Interior Chinatown, New York: Pantheon, Act VI,
quote.text: Your Honor, we object to all of this. The whole thing. This mock trial. The entire justice system is rigged against my client.

definitions.definition: A difficult or annoying experience or person; (especially religion) such an experience seen as a test of faith and piety.

quote.citation: 1678, John Bunyan, The Pilgrim’s Progress‎[7], London: Nath. Ponder, page 172:
quote.text: That they are Cowards, many have said, but few have found it so in the time of Trial.

quote.citation: 1818, Mary Shelley, chapter 5, in Frankenstein‎[8], volume 1, London: Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor, & Jones, page 120:
quote.text: Poor Justine was very ill; but other trials were reserved for her.

quote.citation: 1908, Lucy Maud Montgomery, chapter 12, in Anne of Green Gables‎[9], Toronto: Ryerson Press, page 108:
quote.text: I’m afraid I’m going to be a dreadful trial to you. Maybe you’d better send me back to the asylum.

quote.citation: 1955, J. R. R. Tolkien, chapter 4, in The Return of the King‎[10], New York: Ballantine Books, published 1973, page 98:
quote.text: […]  I’m not used  […]  to waiting hungry on others while they eat. It is a sore trial for a hobbit, that.

quote.citation: 2008, Tan Twan Eng, The Gift of Rain‎[11], New York: Weinstein Books, Book 2, Chapter 13, p. 365:
quote.text: You must be strong now, for your greatest trials are still ahead.

definitions.definition: (archaic) The action of trying (to do) something, especially more than once. (This sense is still current in the expression trial and error.)

quote.citation: 1719, Daniel Defoe, Robinson Crusoe‎[12], London: W. Taylor, page 123:
quote.text: Finding my first Seed did not grow, which I easily imagin’d was by the Drought, I sought for a moister Piece of Ground to make another Trial in,

quote.citation: 1839, Charles Dickens, chapter 28, in Oliver Twist‎[13], volume 2, London: Richard Bentley, page 144:
quote.text: He summoned up all his strength for one last trial, and bent his faltering steps towards [the house].

quote.citation: 1913, Willa Cather, chapter 1, in O Pioneers!‎[14], Boston: Houghton Mifflin, page 18:
quote.text: After a dozen trials he succeeded in lighting the lantern,

quote.citation: 1950, Rachel Carson, chapter 1, in The Sea Around Us‎[15], New York: Oxford University Press, published 1961, page 7:
quote.text: Before the first living cell was created, there may have been many trials and failures.

definitions.definition: Pertaining to a trial or test.
Attempted on a provisional or experimental basis.
(transitive) To carry out a series of tests on (a new product, procedure etc.) before marketing or implementing it.

quote.citation: 2020 April 22, “Network News: Bombardier resumes work at Derby Litchurch Lane”, in Rail, page 9:
quote.text: In the week beginning April 6, the company began trialling the new processes - these include greater spacing, split shifts, additional safety requirements and washing facilities.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To try out (a new player) in a sports team.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Latin tri- (stem of trēs (“three”)) + -al, on the pattern of dual.

definitions.definition: Characterized by having three (usually equivalent) components.
(grammar) Pertaining to a language form referring to three of something, like people. (See Ambai language for an example.)
